name: Enameloplasty (tooth reshaping)
lead: Enameloplasty, also called tooth reshaping, contouring, recontouring, odontoplasty or stripping, is the removal of small amounts of enamel to change a tooth's length, shape or surface, for example to smooth a chip, shorten a pointed canine or even out an uneven edge.[1]

It helps someone look better through the smile: because it changes tooth proportions and symmetry in a single visit, it is used to soften crooked or overly long teeth, harmonise neighbouring teeth of different sizes and sometimes to substitute for braces. Wikipedia's cosmetic-dentistry article describes the results as fast and the procedure as a possible substitute for braces in some circumstances, while noting that removed enamel cannot be replaced and dentin may be exposed.[1]

A 2019 paper on cosmetic recontouring describes enameloplasty of natural teeth as an economical and safe option with esthetic benefits, sometimes combined with additive composite resin.[6] The same word is used in other parts of dentistry, for widening fissures before sealants and for bite adjustments that reduce muscle hyperactivity.[2][3][4][5]
infobox: Dentist; often combined with bonding or orthodontics

paras: Cosmetic enameloplasty alters small details of tooth shape and is listed among cosmetic procedures that remove tooth material.[1] According to the cosmetic-dentistry article, it can fix a small chip or change a tooth's length, shape or position, including crooked or overly long teeth and differences in tooth size.[1] Clinicians may follow it with polishing or direct composite bonding, and a 2019 paper discusses recontouring as an economical option that must also respect function in treatment planning.[6]

A close relative is interproximal enamel reduction (IPR), in which thin layers of enamel are removed between teeth, usually to create space during orthodontic treatment; in a 2025 systematic review of 61 young patients in ten studies, tooth reshaping accounted for 42.6 percent of IPR indications and crowding for 57.4 percent.[7]

Interproximal reduction goes by several other names, including interproximal enamel reduction, slenderising, air-rotor stripping and reproximation. It removes enamel from the contact surfaces between neighbouring teeth to create room for crowded teeth or to reshape contact areas, and is usually followed by recontouring and protection of the treated surfaces.[16]

Wikipedia traces the approach to Murray Ballard, who advocated stripping the lower front teeth in 1944, and says the technique drew renewed interest in the 1980s through John Sheridan's air-rotor stripping, offered as an alternative to extractions or arch expansion. Zachrisson's 2004 work linked the procedure to better front-tooth aesthetics by reducing the dark triangles that can appear between teeth.[16]

Indications listed on Wikipedia include mild to moderate crowding (roughly 4 to 8 mm), dark triangles between front teeth and improving the stability of results after braces. Cases it lists as less suitable include high cavity risk, poor oral hygiene, active gum disease, multiple restorations, large pulp chambers or cold sensitivity.[16]

For amount, the article says that about half of the enamel on a contact surface can reportedly be removed without dental or gum problems, and cites a general guideline of about 0.2 mm per surface on the incisors, with measurements taken before extensive removal.[16] Abrasive metal strips, diamond-coated discs and burs are the instruments described, with water cooling recommended because excess heat can injure the pulp.[16]

Cosmetic uses listed include smoothing chips, correcting overly long or pointed teeth and balancing size differences between teeth.[1] Case reports describe aesthetic correction of unusual tooth forms such as a double tooth, and a 2023 case report of impacted and transposed canines describes multidisciplinary orthodontic planning.[8][9]

In paediatric dentistry, enameloplasty means opening and widening pits and fissures with a bur before placing sealants, and a body of laboratory and clinical work examines sealant penetration and microleakage with and without it.[4][5][10][11] A related 'odontotomy-enameloplasty-sealant' preparation was assessed in a clinical study of 438 occlusal restorations in 124 patients.[12] In occlusal therapy, a computer-guided adjustment technique called immediate complete anterior guidance development has been studied for reducing masseter and temporalis activity.[2][3]

Wikipedia credits Newell Sill Jenkins (1840-1919), an American dentist who worked mostly in Dresden and developed porcelain enamel and inlays, as a founder of aesthetic dentistry.[1] Cosmetic dentistry is not a formal specialty recognised by the American Dental Association, and the article notes criticism that many dentists use the 'cosmetic dentist' label regardless of training; the American Academy of Cosmetic Dentistry, founded in 1984, reports more than 7,000 US members.[1] Teeth whitening is described as the most common cosmetic dental procedure, and clear aligners are an alternative to metal braces.[1]

The cosmetic-dentistry article warns that enamel cannot regrow and dentin can become exposed.[1] The 2025 IPR review used enamel integrity, caries incidence and periodontal status as proxies for safety, and noted that few studies reported follow-up, ranging from 3 to 15 years.[7]

Wikipedia notes that interproximal reduction has been associated with cavities and gum disease, though the link is debated, and that it is irreversible. It describes topical fluoride or a fluoride-varnish retainer as ways dentists reduce risk, and one observational study of 61 people found no gum recession or thinning after 10 or more years in 93 percent. The evidence cited there is largely reviews, laboratory studies and observational work.[16]

No studies found on cosmetic tooth reshaping outcomes for appearance specifically. Related research includes a 2025 systematic review of interproximal enamel reduction in children and adolescents (ten studies, 61 participants, follow-up 3 to 15 years in the few studies reporting it).[7]

Studies of enameloplasty for other purposes include in vitro work on sealant penetration and microleakage in extracted molars, a 2002 study of 30 extracted third molars, a randomised study of enameloplasty sealant technique in fluorosis-affected molars, and a controlled trial of 416 teeth in 162 children aged 6 to 8.[4][5][13][14][15] A 45-subject study of computer-guided enameloplasty reported reduced masseter and temporalis muscle activity.[2] These do not address appearance.

card.summary: Dentist shaves tiny amounts of enamel to alter tooth shape; permanent, and no appearance studies were found.
card.note: Removed enamel does not grow back.

quick.overview:
Enameloplasty is the removal of a little enamel to change how a tooth looks, such as shortening a pointed edge or smoothing a chip.

No clinical studies on the cosmetic use were found; related research concerns sealants and bite adjustment.
quick.mechanism: A dentist uses fine instruments to remove and smooth enamel, changing tooth contours.
quick.risks: Wikipedia says removed enamel is irreplaceable and that dentin may be exposed.

chain: Dentist removes a small amount of enamel with fine burs or discs
Tooth length, edge or contour changes
More even, balanced-looking smile without a long orthodontic course
angle.text: Enameloplasty alters tooth shape in one appointment, so it is used for small chips, uneven edges, pointed teeth and minor size mismatches. Because removed enamel does not regrow, practitioners plan changes conservatively.[1][6]
